The channel description is the highest-leverage sentence you'll write, because it's read only by people deciding whether to subscribe — the exact moment conversion happens. It shows in search results, in the "info" panel, and in the invite preview. Here's what fits, what converts, and 25 examples to adapt.
255 characters
is the hard limit — and the effective budget is smaller: Telegram search and some clients truncate around 120.
No formatting, no links that tap.
A bare @username or URL in the text is not clickable everywhere; put tap-able links in a pinned post instead and reference it.
It's indexed.
Telegram search matches description text, and Google shows it as the snippet for public channels. Keywords here work; keyword stuffed lists read as spam and convert worse.
[Who it's for] + [what they get] + [rhythm/proof].
Three clauses, each doing one job:
"Remote React jobs in Europe, salary listed on every post. New listings daily at 9:00." — who, what, rhythm. 96 characters.
"The 5 AI stories that mattered, with one line on why. Every evening." — filter promise, value-add, rhythm. 74 characters.
"Weekly teardowns of real landing pages. 40,000+ founders read along." — what, proof. 67 characters.
The third clause is swappable: rhythm ("Daily at 9"), proof ("12,000 readers"), or personality ("Written by a human, not a bot"). Pick the one your channel can actually back.
Jobs (5):

"Design jobs with salaries, no agencies. Updated daily." · "Freelance writing gigs in EN. Vetted, posted as they land." · "Internships for CS students in Germany — deadlines never missed." · "QA vacancies, remote first. Weekly digest Fridays." · "Game industry jobs: studios, salaries, referrals."
Deals (5):

"Mistake prices on tech, EU only. Gone in hours — notifications on." · "English books under €5. Kindle and paper." · "Steam sales under €10, rated 80%+." · "Course discounts with expiry dates." · "Refurbished gadgets with warranty, price-checked."
Digests (5):

"AI news filtered to what changes your work. 5 items, every evening." · "EU tech policy in plain language. Mondays." · "Startup funding rounds with the numbers, not the hype." · "Climate news with sources linked. Sundays." · "Space launches, delays included. Live coverage."
Learning (5):

"One English word a day with a real usage example." · "German grammar explained like you're five. B1 in a year." · "SQL lessons in 150 words. Lesson 1 is pinned." · "Design teardowns of apps you use daily." · "A piano piece a week, sheet music included."
Local (5):

"[District] closures, events and power updates. Same day, every time." · "Lisbon rents under €1000, posted daily." · "Subway delays before your commute. Weekdays 7:00." · "Every free event in the city this week. Thursdays." · "Which pharmacy has what. Community-run."
The mission statement.
"We believe information should be free" converts nobody. Describe what arrives in the feed, not why you exist.
The hashtag wall.
#news #crypto #jobs #airdrop signals a channel about everything, which is a channel about nothing.
The empty field.
A blank description says "nobody home" — worse than a mediocre one.
Numbers you can't defend.
"The best channel!" is a claim; "40k readers, 30% open every post" is evidence — only the second converts skeptics.
Common questions
How long can a Telegram channel description be?
255 characters maximum. The first ~120 do most of the work, since search snippets and some clients truncate there — lead with who the channel is for and what it delivers.
Can I add links to my channel description?
You can write a URL, but it is not tappable in every client. Put the links you actually need clicked in a pinned post, and keep the description for the promise.
Does the description help my channel show up in search?
Yes. Telegram search indexes description text alongside the name, and Google uses it as the snippet for public channels. Natural keyword placement helps; stuffing hurts conversion.
